Artificial intelligence lets companies check every transaction instead of a handful. It can also reach where the law forbids. Adamo Brunetti, founder of CODE, explains why the real competitive advantage lies in knowing the difference.

For decades, corporate controls have worked on a simple compromise. Nobody could check everything, so auditors checked a sample and hoped it was representative. That compromise is now disappearing. Artificial intelligence can read every invoice, every payment and every personnel record in real time, and flag the ones that deserve a closer look.

For business leaders, this is good news with a catch. The same technology that makes total control possible also makes it easy to go too far, especially when a company has to investigate its own people. And in Italy, no specific law tells a company how an internal investigation should be conducted.

Adamo Brunetti has spent more than 15 years in compliance and is the founder of CODE. His work focuses on Legislative Decree 231/2001, the Italian law on corporate liability, published 25 years ago, in 2001: he drafts organisational models, sits on supervisory bodies, and has chosen to entrust part of this work to artificial intelligence.

Brunetti did not start in compliance. He began as a white-collar crime lawyer, defending clients in cases arising from business activities, and that experience changed his view of risk. “Whatever the verdict, the trial itself takes a heavy toll on a company, damaging its standing in the market and its financial strength.”

The lesson for any board is clear: by the time a case reaches court, the damage to reputation and financial standing has already been done. The value of compliance lies in acting long before that moment.

His first experiment with AI started with a familiar burden. Supervisory bodies must document every activity, and drafting minutes takes hours. Brunetti built an application, used mainly in house, trained on years of minutes he had written himself and protected by specific safeguards for the confidentiality of the information involved.

“The first time I read minutes drafted by the AI, I was genuinely surprised. They read exactly as if I had written them myself.”

The point is not automation for its own sake. Time once spent on repetitive work now goes into what clients actually pay for: analysing the findings and deciding how to address any non compliance.

You no longer look at a sample. You can look at everything

Traditional audits relied on sampling because human capacity was limited. “The trouble with a sample is that it may only show you what is normal,” Brunetti notes. Finding an anomaly was, in part, a matter of luck, and the most uncomfortable data could easily stay out of view.

Today AI agents connected to company systems, from accounting to human resources, can monitor the entire flow of information and highlight the transactions that deviate from internal procedures. Professionals receive the cases that matter already selected, and can concentrate their judgment where the risk really is. For a company, that means fewer blind spots and a faster response when something goes wrong.

The picture becomes more delicate when a report or a suspicion triggers an internal investigation. Apart from a few specific cases, no primary legislation governs these investigations. Professionals rely on general principles and guidelines, above all the international guidance ISO/TS 37008, which sets out the phases and methods of an investigation according to established practice.

In this grey zone, AI is both a risk and an opportunity. “It is an extremely powerful tool, capable of going places the law does not allow us to go,” Brunetti warns. Used with care, it can search open sources, connect people and events and detect suspicious transactions in a fraction of the time once required. Used carelessly, it can breach the privacy and rights of the people under investigation.

Human dignity is a line you cannot cross, even when you have received a report and have the authority to investigate

For Brunetti, the ultimate boundary lies beyond any single rule. It is human dignity, a principle enshrined in the Italian Constitution and translated into concrete provisions: the Workers’ Statute rules on remote monitoring of employees, and data protection law. Whoever plans an investigation must know these limits from the start.

The stakes are not only ethical. Crossing the line means breaking the law and risking that the evidence gathered becomes unusable. In other words, an investigation conducted without limits can harm the very company that launched it. Respecting those limits protects employees and the business alike.

If knowledge is now available to anyone with an AI assistant, what is left for advisers? Brunetti’s answer is direct. “Until now, consultants have sold a mix of knowledge and experience. Knowledge is now available to anyone. What sets us apart is experience: relationships, trust and the ability to guide clients through strategic decisions that can be critical for an organisation.”

AI also changes how compliance reaches the people who must apply it. Instead of reading long manuals, a manager can describe a specific situation to a chat in natural language and receive the applicable procedure, together with the reasons why it applies. Compliance stops being a binder on a shelf and becomes a tool people actually use.

Three questions for every leadership team

Brunetti’s experience suggests three questions that every board and leadership team should be asking today:

1. Are our controls still based on samples, when the technology to monitor everything already exists?

2. Do we know exactly what an AI tool is allowed to do when we investigate a report, and where the law stops it?

3. Are we using AI to replace judgment, or to give our people more time to exercise it?

Brunetti brought these themes to the stage at SAFE, the Leaders League event held in Milan on 5 November and dedicated to turning risks into business assets.
